Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Overall assessment

**The Seller’s package shifts substantial execution risk and known liabilities to Wattlebridge while weakening its ability to recover after Completion.** The principal concerns are:

- acquiring the business without effective Bluefen consent, clean security releases or verified ownership of key IP;
- paying the AUD 24 million price without appropriate treatment of debt, Completion bonuses and other pre-Completion liabilities; and
- allowing broad disclosure, deemed knowledge and “all Claims” limitations to undermine warranties, indemnities and other remedies.

This review is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter—not the full SPA or underlying DD documents. The Seller’s assertions that matters are “addressed”, “adequate” or “settled” should not be accepted without verification.

## 1. Completion protection: do not accept promises to fix matters afterwards

### Bluefen consent — material customer risk

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The Disclosure Letter confirms there is no final written consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied. The Seller’s statement that consent is “addressed” is therefore unsupported.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen consent a condition precedent, waivable only by the Buyer.
- Require satisfaction of the clause 11.3 conditions, not merely delivery of a document labelled “consent”.
- Require consent on terms acceptable to the Buyer, without adverse changes to pricing, termination rights or other material terms.
- Include a long-stop date and Buyer termination right if the condition remains unsatisfied.

A reasonable-endeavours obligation governs the Seller’s efforts; it is **not a substitute for the required outcome**.

### Riverlark debt and security — discharge at Completion

A release provided after Completion is inconsistent with the Buyer receiving a debt-free business and clean title at Completion. Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding, and change-of-control requirements also need addressing.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a lender payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Repay the facility through the Completion funds flow, with the amount reflected in the debt-free/cash-free price calculation.
- Require effective releases of all relevant security and guarantees at Completion, supported by binding lender undertakings and an agreed registration/discharge process.
- Verify relevant security registrations and any lender consent required pending repayment.

Do not deduct the same debt twice if the price-adjustment mechanism already accounts for it.

### Ironquay IP — payment indemnity is too narrow

The issue is not simply the **AUD 180,000** open balance: transfer of SOW3 Project Materials apparently depends on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. The ledger is not conclusive proof of non-payment, but ownership remains unverified.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all SOW3 fees and obtain evidence of cleared payment.
- Require an effective confirmatory assignment or equivalent evidence establishing the Company’s ownership and necessary rights.
- Check the scope of the materials, relevant contributors and any third-party components.
- Broaden the specific indemnity beyond the payment itself to losses arising from the identified ownership defect, including reasonable rectification, defence and replacement costs.

If the IP is material to operations, resolve ownership before Completion rather than rely solely on damages afterwards.

## 2. Price and funds flow: ensure the Seller bears the right liabilities

### Completion bonuses — AUD 420,000 plus possible on-costs

Calling these “a matter for the Seller” does not protect the Buyer if the Company remains obliged to pay them. Their omission from the funds flow creates a potential additional acquisition cost.

**Push back:**
- Identify the legal payer, recipients, payment timing and precise conditions.
- Determine applicable superannuation, payroll tax, withholding and other on-costs.
- Allocate Seller transaction/Completion bonuses expressly to the Seller through payment, a price deduction or a specific indemnity.
- Distinguish any genuinely negotiated post-Completion retention arrangements benefiting the Buyer.
- Ensure consistent treatment across debt, working capital and transaction-expense definitions, without double counting.

### Sandbar renewals — classification remains unresolved

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. The evidence supplied does not establish that they are ordinary-course costs, unavoidable liabilities or liabilities properly borne by the Seller.

**Push back:**
- Review DD-008 and DD-011 together for commitment dates, coverage periods, cancellation rights and accrual treatment.
- Assess the commitments in aggregate, including whether any pre-Completion consent threshold applies.
- Allocate amounts through the agreed accounting and price mechanics according to their substance.

Reject the Seller’s unsupported classification, but do not automatically deduct the entire amount: genuine future operating costs may properly remain with the business.

## 3. Liability regime: prevent general limitations swallowing specific protection

### General warranty cap and thresholds

A **20% cap—AUD 4.8 million—** is a commercial negotiating position, not necessarily unacceptable in isolation. Its adequacy depends on warranty coverage, exclusions, Seller creditworthiness and available security or insurance.

The proposed combination is materially Seller-friendly:
- individual claims must **exceed AUD 25,000**;
- aggregate qualifying claims must **exceed AUD 250,000**; and
- only the excess above AUD 250,000 is recoverable.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher cap, calibrated to the actual risk allocation.
- Reduce the thresholds and seek a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying losses become recoverable from the first dollar once the threshold is reached.
- Aggregate claims arising from related facts or a common cause.
- Clarify treatment of amounts exactly equal to the thresholds.
- Exclude fundamental warranties, tax protection and agreed specific indemnities from the general thresholds.

A headline cap offers little protection if disclosure and knowledge exclusions remove most claims before the cap matters.

### Fundamental warranties and tax need separate treatment

“Administrative simplicity” is no justification for limiting capacity and title protection to AUD 4.8 million and 18 months. The Buyer could lose its investment while recovering only a fraction of the price.

**Push back:**
- Give capacity, authority, ownership, full title to all shares and freedom from encumbrances a separate regime.
- Seek at least purchase-price-level protection for fundamental claims, with a materially longer survival period.
- Require a separate tax covenant/indemnity covering appropriately allocated pre-Completion tax, with tailored exclusions and claims procedures.
- Set tax survival by reference to relevant assessment/reassessment periods, with a notification buffer—not the general 18-month deadline.

IP warranties should also be reviewed independently; the Seller’s assertion that they are settled does not resolve Ironquay or establish that the wider IP protection is adequate.

### “All Claims” wording threatens the entire bargain

Applying caps, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to **all Claims of any nature** could restrict:
- specific indemnities and tax claims;
- payment and price-adjustment obligations;
- pre-Completion covenant breaches;
- fundamental claims; and
- misrepresentation and other available remedies.

**Push back:**
- Replace blanket application with an express claim-by-claim allocation.
- Ensure specific indemnities are not defeated by disclosure, Buyer knowledge or general warranty limitations.
- Preserve appropriate rights to enforce payment obligations, obtain specific performance or injunctions, and exercise termination rights.
- Include express protection for fraud and deliberate concealment, with careful attribution drafting, and preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.

Review clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 together: improving one provision is ineffective if another reinstates the exclusion.

### Time limits and claim procedure

Eighteen months may leave little time to identify problems across a complete reporting cycle.

Seek a longer general warranty period, commonly negotiated at **24 months**, with longer tailored periods for fundamental and tax claims. Also check that reasonable claim notification preserves a claim despite unquantified loss, and that short proceedings deadlines or technical notice requirements do not extinguish it prematurely.

## 4. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: reject deemed omniscience

General disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room, accounts, registers and public records is too broad. It risks treating obscure documents and external references as disclosure of their legal significance.

Clause 8.3 goes further by treating matters **discoverable** by the Buyer or its advisers as known.

**Push back:**
- Require fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter.
- Link specific disclosures to relevant warranties.
- Reject wholesale deemed disclosure of public records and material merely referred to in documents.
- Freeze and retain an agreed, indexed data-room copy.
- Delete constructive knowledge and blanket adviser-knowledge attribution; any compromise should be confined to actual knowledge of named individuals.
- Require updated disclosures before Completion, with Buyer rights over material new matters rather than automatic qualification of repeated warranties.

**Disclosure is not remediation.** A disclosed risk may cease to support a warranty claim, making a specific indemnity, price adjustment or Completion condition especially important.

## 5. Other material diligence points

### Export/privacy incident

The record establishes a misdirected download link and a potentially affected dataset—not confirmed unauthorised access, a legally notifiable breach or quantified loss. Equally, “not expected to be material” is unsupported while the investigation is preliminary.

Require:
- containment and preservation of evidence;
- investigation of access, dataset scope, recipient actions and applicable legal/contractual notification duties;
- appropriate remediation and controlled notification arrangements; and
- a specific indemnity for the identified pre-Completion incident, with suitable investigation and claims-control provisions.

Do not treat AUD zero reported loss as evidence of no exposure.

### Lease and Mossvale

Avoid imposing unsupported consent requirements:
- **Office lease:** verify and comply with the notification obligation; the supplied material does not establish landlord consent is required.
- **Mossvale:** a restriction on assignment does not itself establish a consent requirement for a share sale. Review the full contract for separate change-of-control provisions.

### Share title

DD-012 is evidence of registered ownership, not complete proof of clean title. Verify the issued capital, constitution, share certificates and issue/transfer history, together with any options, competing rights, encumbrances and transfer restrictions. Require effective transfers and registration of the Buyer at Completion.

## Recommended negotiating position

1. **Completion gates:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment and releases, and verified ownership of material Ironquay IP.
2. **Protect the price:** reconcile debt, bonuses and on-costs, and supplier commitments in one consistent funds flow.
3. **Separate liability regimes:** preserve meaningful fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity protection outside general warranty restrictions.
4. **Reject blanket exclusions:** narrow disclosure, knowledge, non-reliance and “all Claims” wording.
5. **Resolve identified uncertainty:** investigate the export incident and obtain current evidence rather than accept Seller characterisations.
6. **Secure recoverability:** assess Seller covenant strength and negotiate retention, escrow or other security where warranted.

**Do not sign off on the package until these protections are reflected consistently across the SPA, Disclosure Letter and Completion deliverables.**
